lesson.title: insert(): Placing an Item Exactly Where You Want It
lesson.summary: How .insert(index, item) adds an element at a specific position, shifting everything after it to the right, and what happens when the index is out of range.
lesson.body:
append only ever adds to the end of a list, which is fast and simple but not always what you need. Sometimes a new item belongs at the very front, or somewhere in the middle, and for that Python provides insert, which lets you name the exact position where the new element should land.

The syntax is list.insert(index, item). Unlike append, insert takes two arguments: the position where item should end up, and the item itself. Every element that was already sitting at that index, and every element after it, gets shifted one position to the right to make room. Like append, insert mutates the list in place and returns None.

tasks = ["wake up", "eat breakfast", "leave for school"]
tasks.insert(1, "brush teeth")
print(tasks)

tasks.insert(0, "turn off alarm")
print(tasks)

tasks.insert(100, "go to bed")
print(tasks)

Trace each step. tasks starts as ["wake up", "eat breakfast", "leave for school"]. tasks.insert(1, "brush teeth") places "brush teeth" at index 1, pushing "eat breakfast" and "leave for school" one spot to the right, giving ["wake up", "brush teeth", "eat breakfast", "leave for school"], which is what the first print shows. tasks.insert(0, "turn off alarm") places the new item at the very front, index 0, shifting everything else right by one, giving ["turn off alarm", "wake up", "brush teeth", "eat breakfast", "leave for school"].

The third call is the interesting one: tasks.insert(100, "go to bed") asks for index 100, but the list only has five elements, indices 0 through 4. Python does not raise an error here the way indexing with fruits[100] would. Instead, insert clamps an out-of-range index to the nearest valid boundary, so an index that is too large simply appends the item to the end, exactly as if you had called append. The result is ["turn off alarm", "wake up", "brush teeth", "eat breakfast", "leave for school", "go to bed"], with the new task tacked on last.

Negative indices work with insert too, following the same rule you learned for list indexing: insert(-1, item) inserts item at the position of the current last element, pushing that former last element one spot further right rather than putting the new item after it.

colors = ["red", "green", "blue"]
colors.insert(-1, "yellow")
print(colors)

Here -1 refers to "blue", the current last element, sitting at index 2. Inserting "yellow" at that position shifts "blue" to index 3, giving ["red", "green", "yellow", "blue"], not ["red", "green", "blue", "yellow"] as you might first guess. This is a common point of confusion, so it is worth testing in your head before you rely on it: insert(-1, x) means "put x right before the last item," never "put x after the last item," since that second job belongs to append.

One practical note for later, more advanced work: because insert has to shift every element after the target position, inserting near the front of a very long list is slower than appending to the end, an operation whose cost grows with how many elements need to move rather than staying constant like append's does.
